analysis.one_liner: Makes health plans prove their mental health coverage rules are as fair as their physical health rules.
analysis.headline: The bill cleared a House committee by voice vote and was placed on the House calendar in December 2020, but the House never voted on it before the 116th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Federal law already says insurance plans must cover mental health and substance use treatment at the same level as physical medical care. In practice, plans often get around this with rules that are hard to measure — like requiring prior approval, limiting which therapists are in the network, or setting medical-necessity criteria that favor physical care. This bill would force plans to document, on request to the government, exactly how they design and apply those rules and to show that they are no more restrictive than the rules for physical care. Plans found out of compliance would have to fix the problem within 45 days or notify everyone enrolled in the plan, and the government would issue annual public reports naming noncompliant plans.
analysis.who_benefits: People who need mental health or substance use treatment: they would gain a way to challenge narrower networks, higher cost-sharing, prior-authorization hurdles, and "fail-first" drug policies that plans apply more aggressively to mental health than to physical care. Providers of mental health services would also benefit from fuller networks and clearer coverage rules.
analysis.who_benefits_short: People needing mental health or addiction treatment

how_it_helps.text: It requires plans to prove, on request, that restrictions on mental health and substance use care — medical necessity criteria, prior-authorization rules, fail-first protocols, network admission standards — are no more restrictive than the rules they apply to physical medical and surgical care.

Plans found out of compliance must fix the problem within 45 days or notify every person enrolled in the plan that it was found noncompliant, and the government must publish an annual report naming noncompliant plans.

Plans must disclose the reasons for any denial of mental health coverage and the medical-necessity criteria to enrollees and providers, and must cover out-of-network mental health providers if they cover out-of-network doctors for physical care.

analysis.who_pays: Health insurers and large employer group plans, which would face compliance documentation, government review, public naming of violators, and potentially higher costs from expanded mental health coverage. Some of that cost could flow into premiums shared by workers, and the bill's small-employer exemption leaves small business plans unaffected.
analysis.who_pays_short: Health insurers and large employer plans

drawbacks.text: The bill includes a cost exemption: a plan can escape the parity requirements for a plan year if a certified actuary determines compliance would raise total costs by more than 2% the first year and 1% in later years, and the employer can elect this exemption repeatedly — a loophole insurers could use to delay compliance.
Employers and insurers would bear compliance and administrative costs, and some plans could see modestly higher premiums, which may be passed to workers through their share of coverage costs.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real but conditional: enforcement of parity rules has failed for over a decade, and disclosure with annual agency reviews and public naming of violators is a tested way to change plan behavior. The main costs are higher premiums where compliance requires richer mental health coverage, and the bill's own cost-increase exemption lets a plan avoid the rules for a year with an actuary's certification — a loophole an insurer could use, softened only by the notification and audit requirements.

outcome.mechanism: It passed a House committee by voice vote and was placed on the House calendar, but House leaders never brought it up for a floor vote before Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: The House Energy and Commerce Committee reported the bill on July 15, 2020, by voice vote, and formally reported it on December 24, 2020.
On December 24, 2020, the bill was placed on the Union Calendar (Calendar No. 575), the step that makes a bill eligible for a House floor vote.
No floor vote ever occurred; the action history ends at placement on the calendar, and the 116th Congress expired on January 3, 2021.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Health insurers and large employer plans keep the discretion to apply stricter rules to mental health coverage without having to document or justify them, and the status quo of uneven parity enforcement continued.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Insurers and large employer health plans

sides.party_line_note: The bill's sponsor and cosponsors split evenly between the parties — three Democrats and three Republicans — and it cleared committee on a voice vote, indicating no recorded opposition in committee.

industries.note: The bill requires insurers and group plans to document and defend every restriction they place on mental health and substance use care and to prove it is no tighter than their rules for physical care, with public naming of violators. That targets the techniques insurers use to limit mental health spending.

Large self-insured employer plans must perform and produce comparative parity analyses and can face compliance findings, adding administrative burden, though a cost-increase exemption lets them opt out for a year if compliance raises costs by more than 2% the first year and 1% thereafter.
